title.full: ASEAN Green Future Project Phase 2.2 Report, Optimising Malaysia's Electrifying Future

publisher.full: Sustainable Development Solutions Network and ClimateWorks Centre

description: Normative MY least-cost power pathway to 100% renewables by 2050 with full fossil phase-out.
pathwayDescription:
Normative Malaysian pathway reaching a 100% renewable power system by 2050: no new fossil capacity after 2030, coal phased out early and gas and diesel by 2050, plus stronger efficiency standards. Least-cost optimization picks 81 GW solar, 24 GW biomass, hydro, batteries, and pumped hydro. Power emissions fall from 87 to 2 MtCO2e, but investment rises to US$393B (1.8x OEP) and the biomass build far exceeds assessed resource potential.

The ASEAN Green Future regional research project is run by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network, Climateworks Centre, and local researchers from leading universities. The project develops national policy analysis and near-zero pathways that are meant to provide policy recommendations and support policymakers.

coreDrivers.policies: There is no new fossil capacity after 2030. Coal is phased out by 2030, and gas and diesel by 2050. 100% renewable power is targeted.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: The pathway is constrained to a near-zero emissions, 100% renewable power sector by 2050, implemented through fuel phaseout and no-new-fossil constraints rather than an explicit emissions cap. Power emissions fall to 2 MtCO2e in 2050.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: OMAP is a cost-optimized pathway within the fossil-free 2050 constraint. The optimizer selects 23.9 GW biomass (125 TWh), 13.6 GW large and 4.2 GW small hydro, 81 GW solar, 5.3 GW wind, 4.5 GW batteries, and 8.0 GW pumped hydro.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: This scenario requires US$393B investment in power generation capacity, 1.8 times more than the OEP pathway.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: OMAP uses the same GDP, population, urbanization, and sectoral value-added assumptions as EP and OEP; its 2050 electricity demand of 369 TWh (+137% vs. 2019) is about 6% below EP because of efficiency measures, not different macro assumptions.
coreDrivers.behavioralShifts: Commercial energy-intensity gain doubles to 46% compared to EP and OEP. Industry energy intensity improvement is 23% plus a 4% circular-economy steel demand cut, with electricity’s fuel share raised to 46%; efficient household appliances at 100% by 2060.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Biomass as a resource is left unconstrained. The report says this result must be triangulated with a land-use study.

dependencies.dependency_description: OMAP rests on commitments absent from today's plans — no new fossil capacity after 2030, coal exit by 2030, gas and diesel exit by 2050, 100% renewable power, a doubled commercial efficiency target (46%) and a 46% industrial electricity share. Without them the least-cost solution reverts to the OEP gas-heavy mix. The report's recommendations include a roadmap for retiring uncontracted gas and coal plants, biomass and biogas incentives, and support for pumped hydro.

OMAP needs rules that let storage and interconnection scale: the report recommends remuneration for flexibility services, technology-neutral storage evaluation, streamlined pumped-hydro permitting with long-term revenue visibility, and harmonised grid codes and standards for regional power trade. With 8.0 GW of pumped hydro and 4.5 GW of batteries, these rules bind more than in EP or OEP (evidence-based inference from storage capacity).

OMAP needs 1.8x OEP's investment (US$393B real) and raises 2050 production cost to 10.6 US cents/kWh, against current tariffs of 4.2–12.0 US cents/kWh. Its economic case depends on carbon pricing: from US$185/t it has the lowest social cost (Table 7), and Malaysia's carbon tax on iron/steel and energy from 2026 is noted. The report also calls for grants, tax breaks and green finance for pumped hydro and biomass plantations.

OMAP raises large hydro to 13.6 GW, small hydro to 4.2 GW and biomass to 23.9 GW. The report warns that hydropower can displace indigenous communities and that biomass expansion must respect land rights and sustainability to win social and political acceptance; large-hydro growth warrants environmental impact assessment.

On top of EP's transport assumptions, OMAP requires 100% efficient lighting, refrigeration and air conditioning by 2060 and a 46% commercial efficiency gain, cutting 2050 demand 6% versus EP (369 vs. 393 TWh) and residential demand 11%. Commercial uptake is the weak link, since the EECA covers only 21% of commercial consumption; these are imposed adoption assumptions rather than modeled behaviour.

A 100% renewable system needs 4.5 GW of batteries (less than 1GW in OEP or EP) and 8.0 GW of pumped hydro (1.96 GWh per million people), 2.8 GW of offshore wind, and transmission from renewable zones to load centres; the cheapest decarbonization route needs a coordinated regional approach and proposes a UHV DC backbone. Storage and transmission are preconditions for OMAP. Only annual capacity results are reported, with no hourly dispatch, which limits curtailment assessment.

OMAP relies on 4.5 GW of batteries alongside pumped hydro. This is only 0.76 GW in OEP scenario. The report states storage costs may hold back further solar within the least-cost framework and that future battery cost declines could favour more solar, and cites studies requiring at least eight hours of storage at high renewable shares. So battery cost and duration improvements are a key enabling factor.

OMAP removes gas imports but shifts the binding resource to land and feedstock: 23.9 GW of biomass generating 125 TWh far exceeds SEDA's 2.3 GW biomass potential, and large hydro reaches SEDA's 13.6 GW large-hydro potential. The report calls for a land-use study, dedicated tree plantations and sustainable supply chains, noting biomass crops can need 29–154 times more land than solar per unit of electricity.

About 38% of OMAP's 2050 generation is hydro and 30% biomass, both flagged as more vulnerable to climate impacts such as drought; solar and hydro availability across the two monsoon seasons was not tested. Large hydro needs environmental impact assessment and biomass must account for biodiversity, soil health and water; pumped hydro needs about 3 litres of water per person per day.

The report notes that Malaysian tree planters struggle with labour and profitability, which matters for the plantation-based biomass supply OMAP's 23.9 GW would need; it does not quantify power-sector workforce needs.
